title: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
answer: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review cover the use of machine learning to classify, rank, and prioritize documents in large-scale e-discovery and document analysis. The scope includes relevance review, privilege screening, issue tagging, and quality control across collections that may run into millions of items. It also covers the workflows that surround the model, such as sampling, validation, and the documentation needed to explain how a production set was built. sections.body: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review cover the use of machine learning to classify, rank, and prioritize documents in large-scale e-discovery and document analysis. The scope includes relevance review, privilege screening, issue tagging, and quality control across collections that may run into millions of items. It also covers the workflows that surround the model, such as sampling, validation, and the documentation needed to explain how a production set was built. The topic sits inside e-discovery and large-scale document analysis, so it touches litigation, internal investigations, regulatory responses, and data subject access requests.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on document review platforms that combine storage, indexing, optical character recognition, deduplication, and search. They may be deployed in a cloud environment or on premises, depending on the matter's data handling rules and the client's security posture. The infrastructure also includes load files, metadata fields, review queues, and audit logs that connect the model's output to the documents a reviewer sees. Compute needs are modest compared with training large language models, but the collection size, the number of iterations, and the need for responsive review interfaces drive the design.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually begins with a seed set or a small sample of documents coded by a subject matter expert, which trains a classifier to rank the remaining collection by likely relevance. Reviewers then code documents in iterative rounds, and the model updates its ranking, a pattern often called continuous active learning. Teams monitor precision, recall, and elusion, which is an estimate of how much relevant material remains in the unreviewed pool. The final steps include quality control, privilege review, and a defensible record of the training and review decisions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on defensibility, proportionality, and the protection of privileged or personal data. Teams need to document the protocol, the seed set, the model versions, the sampling plan, and the reasons for stopping review, because opposing parties and courts may ask how the process was conducted. Provenance matters, so audit trails should link each produced document to its review history and to the model that ranked it. The site tracks 29 AI case law precedents and 222 compliance and regulation pages, and e-discovery teams watch those developments because they shape how much explanation and validation a court may expect.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward tighter integration with generative AI, which can summarize documents, draft privilege logs, and help reviewers navigate large productions. Continuous learning and active learning are likely to become more automated, with less manual seed set work and more emphasis on monitoring for drift and bias. Standards and case law will continue to develop around transparency, validation, and the use of large language models in review. The practical effect is that e-discovery professionals will spend more time on protocol design, quality control, and explaining model behavior, and less time on first-pass relevance coding.
